chapters.title: Chapter 2: Reading Where India Is in the Cycle

lessons.title: The RBI Rate Cycle and Liquidity: The Clock Behind the Cycle

body.text: The RBI does not create the business cycle, but it sets its clock. Rate cuts and easy liquidity start the recovery; hikes and tight liquidity end the expansion. Learn to read the clock, and you know which part of the cycle the sectors are pricing.

children.text: Every episode in Chapter 1 had the RBI at its centre: 425 basis points of cuts in the 2008 crisis, 375 basis points of hikes by 2011, the repo rate at 4% during Covid, and 250 basis points of hikes in 2022 to 2023. This lesson explains how that policy machine works, why its effects arrive with long lags, and how to use the rate cycle as a timing tool for sector rotation.
How the RBI Runs Monetary Policy

markDefs.definition: The MPC's signal about the likely direction of future policy. "Accommodative" signals that cuts or easy conditions are likely, "neutral" signals that the next move could go either way, and a tightening stance signals possible hikes.

children.text: Since 2016, India has followed flexible inflation targeting. The government sets the target, and a six-member Monetary Policy Committee, three from the RBI and three external members, decides the policy repo rate. The target is CPI inflation of 4%, with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%. On 25 March 2026, the government retained that same target for the five years from April 2026 to March 2031. Alongside the rate decision, the MPC announces its
policy stance
, which is often a better guide to the next six to twelve months than the rate move itself.

cells: The rate at which the RBI lends overnight to banks against government securities. The headline policy rate.
The rate at which banks can park surplus funds with the RBI without collateral. The floor of the policy corridor since April 2022.
Emergency overnight borrowing for banks at a penalty rate. The ceiling of the corridor.
The share of deposits banks must keep with the RBI, earning no interest. Changing it adds or drains durable liquidity.
3% of net demand and time liabilities, after 100 bps of cuts in 2025
Open market operations and FX swaps
Buying or selling government bonds, or swapping dollars for rupees, to inject or absorb liquidity.
Forward guidance on the likely direction of rates.

body.label: The operating target
body.context: The overnight interbank rate the RBI aims to keep close to the repo rate, inside the 50 bps corridor between the SDF and the MSF. When the call rate drifts towards the SDF, liquidity is in surplus; when it drifts towards the MSF, liquidity is tight.

children.text: The Rate Cycle Clock
Rate cycles in India follow a recognisable sequence. The stance usually changes before the rate does, and a pause is its own distinct phase, not just an absence of action.

body.caption: The RBI rate cycle, step by step

cells: Stance shifts towards accommodative; first cuts
Growth slowing, inflation falling or within target
Bond yields fall; rate sensitive stocks start to anticipate recovery
Large or rapid cuts, liquidity injections, CRR cuts
Markets often bottom here, long before the economy
Rates on hold, stance moves to neutral
Leadership broadens from rate sensitives to cyclicals
Rate sensitives lose momentum; yields rise
Rates on hold at the top
Defensives tend to outperform; markets look for the first cut

body.title: RBI repo rate at every change, June 2018 to December 2025 (%)

children.text: The chart shows each change, so the spacing on the axis is not proportional to time. The two long gaps are the story: the repo rate sat at 4% for two years from May 2020 to May 2022, and then at 6.5% for two years from February 2023 to February 2025. Pauses at the bottom and at the top can last longer than the cutting or hiking phases themselves.

events.title: Second cut, stance turns accommodative

events.description: Repo cut by 25 bps to 5.25%, bringing total easing in 2025 to 125 bps.

events.title: Fourth straight pause
events.description: Repo held at 5.25% with a neutral stance, citing global uncertainty. The RBI projects FY27 growth at 6.7% and inflation at 5.0%.

body.text: Notice the stance in June 2025. The RBI cut by a large 50 bps, but at the same time moved the stance from accommodative back to neutral. That was a signal that the easing cycle was being front-loaded and was closer to its end than its beginning. Stance changes like this are often the clearest hint that the clock is about to move to the next position.

children.text: Why Policy Works With Long Lags

A rate cut does not lift growth the next morning. It first has to pass through money markets, bank deposit and lending rates, borrowing decisions, spending, hiring, and prices. IMF research on India estimates that a policy rate increase starts to weigh on output growth after about two quarters and on inflation after about three quarters, with effects lasting eight to ten quarters. That is why the RBI sets policy on its forecasts rather than on today's inflation, and why markets try to front-run both.

markDefs.definition: A publicly visible rate, in practice usually the RBI repo rate, to which a bank links its floating loan interest rate. When the benchmark changes, the loan rate resets within a defined period, unlike older internal benchmarks such as MCLR that banks calculated from their own cost of funds.

children.text: Liquidity: The Second Hand of the Clock

markDefs.definition: The net amount of surplus or deficit funds in the banking system, measured by how much banks park with or borrow from the RBI under its liquidity operations. A surplus pushes short-term market rates towards the floor of the corridor; a deficit pushes them towards the ceiling.

children.text: Rates are only half the story. The other half is
system liquidity

, the amount of spare cash in the banking system. The RBI can keep the repo rate unchanged yet tighten or ease conditions sharply by draining or adding liquidity. In practice, it often moves liquidity first: tightening liquidity before the first hike, and injecting it before or alongside cuts.

Easy liquidity: call rates trade near or below the repo rate, banks cut deposit rates, and bond yields and corporate borrowing costs fall. Good for lenders' funding costs and for rate sensitive borrowers.

Tight liquidity: call rates push up towards the MSF, short-term borrowing costs rise even without a hike, and banks compete for deposits. Tough for NBFCs and companies that depend on short-term market funding.
Is Policy Actually Loose or Tight?
A 5.25% repo rate means nothing on its own. What matters to borrowers and savers is the rate after inflation. The simplest gauge is the real policy rate.

body.caption: Use a forward-looking inflation estimate, such as the RBI's own projection, rather than last month's print

body.title: Calculate the Real Policy Rate
body.prompt: In August 2026, the repo rate is 5.25% and the RBI projects CPI inflation of 5.0% for FY27. What is the approximate real policy rate, in percent?
body.explanation: 5.25% minus 5.0% is about 0.25%. A real rate close to zero is relatively accommodative. Many economists estimate India's neutral real rate, the level that neither stimulates nor restrains growth, somewhere around 1% to 2%, though estimates vary. Note that a real rate that looked comfortably positive when inflation was expected to be lower can shrink quickly if inflation forecasts rise, even without any change in the repo rate.

body.title: Go deeper: a simple rule of thumb for where rates "should" be

children.text: Economists often benchmark central bank decisions against a Taylor-type rule. It says the policy rate should rise when inflation is above target and when the economy is running above potential, and fall when the opposite is true.

content.caption: i = suggested policy rate, r* = neutral real rate, π = expected inflation, π* = inflation target (4% for India)

content.title: Apply the Rule
content.prompt: Assume a neutral real rate of 1.5%, expected inflation of 5%, an inflation target of 4%, and an output gap of minus 0.5%. What policy rate does the rule suggest? (These are illustrative inputs, not an estimate of current conditions.)
content.explanation: 1.5 + 5 + 0.5 x (5 minus 4) + 0.5 x (minus 0.5) = 1.5 + 5 + 0.5 minus 0.25 = 6.75%. The rule is useful for asking whether policy looks loose or tight relative to a simple benchmark. It is not a forecast: the neutral rate and output gap are unobservable estimates, and central banks also weigh supply shocks such as crude oil and food prices, the rupee, and global rates, which the rule ignores.

Signs that inflation is turning up
Banks early on, as loan yields reprice upwards
Real estate, autos, NBFCs, highly indebted companies
The size and speed of hikes; liquidity being drained
FMCG, pharma, and other low-debt defensives

body.text: These are tendencies seen across many cycles, not rules. Chapter 3 examines each sector group in detail, and Chapter 4 tests whether the patterns actually held on Nifty sectoral index data.

children.text: Practice

body.title: Margins in a Cutting Cycle
body.question: The RBI cuts the repo rate by 100 bps over a year. Bank A has 85% of its floating rate loans linked to the repo rate; Bank B has most of its loans on MCLR. Both fund themselves mainly with term deposits. What is most likely in the first few quarters?
options: Both banks see their net interest margins expand equally
Bank A's margins come under more pressure than Bank B's, because its loan yields fall faster than its deposit costs
Bank B's margins fall faster, because MCLR loans reprice immediately
Rate cuts never affect bank margins
body.explanation: Repo-linked loans reset quickly after each cut, while term deposits reprice only as they mature. So a bank with mostly repo-linked loans sees loan yields fall faster than its cost of funds, squeezing margins early in the cycle. MCLR-linked loans adjust gradually, cushioning Bank B for longer. Over time, as deposits reprice and credit growth picks up, the squeeze typically eases.

body.title: Name the Floor
body.textWithBlank: Since April 2022, the floor of the RBI's policy corridor has been the ___, a collateral-free facility where banks park surplus funds overnight at 25 bps below the repo rate.
body.explanation: The Standing Deposit Facility replaced the fixed rate reverse repo as the floor of the liquidity adjustment facility corridor in April 2022. The Marginal Standing Facility, at 25 bps above repo, is the ceiling.

body.title: Where Is the Clock?
body.scenario: The RBI has held the repo rate for four consecutive meetings after a cutting cycle, with a neutral stance. Its inflation projection for next year has just risen from 4.2% to 5.0% because of higher crude oil prices, and the 10-year government bond yield has climbed about 50 bps over a year. Growth forecasts have been raised slightly. You hold a portfolio tilted towards real estate and housing finance companies, bought during the cutting cycle.
body.prompt: Where on the rate cycle clock does this look like, and how should it change the way you think about your sector tilt?
body.modelAnswer: This looks like a pause at the low that is beginning to age. Cuts are over, the stance is neutral, growth is holding up, and inflation expectations are rising. The real policy rate is shrinking as projected inflation rises towards the repo rate, and rising long bond yields are already tightening financial conditions for borrowers even without an RBI hike. The tailwind that favoured real estate and housing finance, falling rates, has ended and could reverse if the RBI starts withdrawing liquidity or signals a tighter stance. That does not mean selling automatically, but it is a reason to revisit the tilt: check how much of the thesis depended on further rate cuts, watch the next policy statement for a change in stance or in liquidity operations, and consider whether position sizes still fit a phase where the rate cycle is no longer helping.

cards.definition: The RBI's policy rate for overnight lending to banks against government securities. 5.25% as of September 2026.
Signals the RBI is prepared to cut rates or keep conditions easy to support growth.
Signals the next move could be a cut or a hike, depending on data.
Cash Reserve Ratio: the share of deposits banks must hold with the RBI. Cut to 3% in 2025, releasing about ₹2.5 lakh crore.
External Benchmark Lending Rate: floating loan rates linked to an external benchmark, usually the repo rate, so they reprice quickly.
The repo rate minus expected inflation. The better gauge of whether policy is actually loose or tight.

body.label: Reserve Bank of India
body.description: Official monetary policy statements, MPC minutes, and the Monetary Policy Report, which carries the RBI's growth and inflation projections.

body.text: This lesson is educational and explains how monetary policy works. It is not investment advice. Policy settings described are as of September 2026 and will change; always check the RBI's latest statement.

points: The MPC targets 4% CPI inflation within a 2% to 6% band, a target retained in March 2026 for April 2026 to March 2031
The rate cycle moves through easing, deep easing, a pause at the low, tightening, and peak rates; stance changes usually come before rate changes
Pauses matter: the repo rate stayed at 4% from May 2020 to May 2022 and at 6.5% from February 2023 to February 2025
The RBI cut the repo rate by 125 bps in 2025 to 5.25% and cut CRR to 3%, then held rates through August 2026
Policy works with long lags, roughly two quarters for output and three for inflation, so markets front-run the RBI
External benchmark linked loans, 61% of floating rate loans by December 2024, speed up transmission but can squeeze bank margins early in a cutting cycle
Use liquidity and the real policy rate, not just the repo rate, to judge whether conditions are actually easing or tightening
